Subject: MSA + Order Form: ops SLA carve-outs and emergency maintenance language

Hi Kimberly,

Thanks for sending the latest MSA + Order Form. We reviewed the operational SLA sections with engineering and legal and have two substantive asks before we can sign:

1) Emergency maintenance carve-outs: we need explicit language allowing us to require a 48-hr notice for emergency maintenance that impacts PII-processing endpoints. The current draft allows Redwood to schedule emergency maintenance with only "reasonable notice" which our security/compliance team can't accept without a carve-out.

2) Service credit cap: AeroHealth will not accept a plan where total monthly credits could exceed 25% of fees in aggregate if the underlying uptime is below provider threshold; we prefer a defined credit matrix capped at 15% so our finance team can forecast.

I've attached a redline showing our suggested edits (redline_orderform_20290610.pdf) and a quick support matrix outlining required response SLAs for P1/P2 incidents.

Can you confirm whether Redwood can:
- Add a clause that requires 48-hr notice for any emergency maintenance that affects endpoints marked as "sensitive" in Schedule B; and
- Consider capping credits at 15% (we can do a 10% cap for the first 6 months as trial but need a maximum documented)?

Appreciate a quick reply — legal would like to aim for signature by 2029-06-20.

Best,
Jordan
Director of Cloud Ops
AeroHealth

Subject: Re: MSA + Order Form: ops SLA carve-outs and emergency maintenance language

Jordan — thanks for the clear note and the redlines. Looping in Lauren (legal) and Marcus (product ops) & Dev (SRE) so we can get a consolidated view.

Quick take from product/SRE:
- Emergency maintenance: we understand the need for more notice when PII is in play. We can add a Schedule B mechanism that flags "sensitive" endpoints and triggers a 48-hr minimum notice for planned maintenance; emergency maintenance (exploit/zero-day mitigation) still needs the ability to be executed with shorter notice in cases where immediate action is required to prevent live compromise.
- As a compromise we can add a clause that requires Redwood to provide as much notice as practicable and, for sensitive endpoints, a minimum of 48 hours for non-critical emergency action; for immediate remediation we propose a post-action review and a 1:1 executive notification within 2 hours.

On credits: Marcus — can you evaluate whether we can accept a 15% cap and what the cost/credit modeling looks like for high-severity incidents?

I will have a legal-proposed redline back to you by EOD tomorrow. If we can get alignment on the emergency carve-out language, we may be able to accept AeroHealth's suggested credit cap subject to the modelling.

Thanks,
Kimberly
Account Executive, Redwood Inference

Jordan / Kimberly / team —

Thanks for the draft asks. Attached is Redwood's proposed wording for Section 5.2 (Maintenance and Emergency Responses) and an alternate formulation for the service credit matrix (both in the attached redline PDF). Key points we propose:

- Definition block: add "Sensitive Endpoint" definition referencing Schedule B (encrypted PII, regulated processing).
- Planned maintenance: standard notice 7 days, with windows defined (02:00-05:00 UTC typical).
- Emergency maintenance: define two tiers — 
  * Tier A (Immediate Threat): Redwood may perform emergency maintenance without prior notice where there is a demonstrated active exploitation risk. Redwood will notify Customer within 2 hours and provide a post-action report within 72 hours.
  * Tier B (Operational Emergency affecting Sensitive Endpoints): Redwood will provide at least 48 hours notice unless doing so materially increases risk; if immediate action is required, Redwood will provide notification as soon as practicable and schedule a follow-up review with Customer within 2 business days.
- Service credits: propose a capped matrix with a sliding scale up to 15% of monthly fees, with an initial 6-month pilot where cap is 10% if both parties agree. Credits are calculated on a pro-rata basis and exclude scheduled maintenance and the emergency exceptions above.

We also propose adding a requirement for a monthly incident summary for any incidents affecting sensitive endpoints and quarterly compliance syncs for the first year post-deployment.

Please review the attached redline and let us know if the Tier A/B split works for AeroHealth.

Regards,
Lauren Bishop
Senior Counsel, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: MSA + Order Form: ops SLA carve-outs and emergency maintenance language

Lauren / Kimberly — thanks, that Tier A/B approach is sensible and addresses our main concern about PII endpoints. A few clarifications from legal & ops:

- The 2-hour notification commitment for Tier A is okay as long as Redwood also confirms the expected customer impact window in that notice (estimated downtime or degraded throughput).
- For Tier B, AeroHealth needs the 48-hr notice to include a proposed maintenance playbook and rollback plan; if Redwood intends to perform immediate action less than 48 hours, we want an explicit one-time exception to be documented with justification and a right to escalate to an executive contact who can pause the action for up to 4 hours while the parties coordinate.
- Credits: AeroHealth accepts the 15% cap but asks that there be an annual review clause to reopen the cap if there are repeated regressions (>3 P1 incidents in any rolling 90-day window).

If Redwood can accept those clarifications, we're close to sending this to procurement to finish paperwork. We aim for signature 2029-06-18.

Thanks,
Jordan
Director of Cloud Ops, AeroHealth
